# Plugin media delivery

The shared desktop/web iframe loader previously allowed only blob/data images and fonts. It had no media-src or media capability. This adds a bounded host delivery capability without network or arbitrary filesystem grants.

A view declares `capabilities.mediaDelivery: {types: ["video/mp4", "image/png"]}`. Its backend looks up an already-produced file (never starts paid work) with `mediaFile(id) -> {path, contentType, fileName?}`. The relative path is interpreted only inside the host-selected plugin data directory. The iframe calls `ct.media(id)` and receives `{handle, url, content_type, file_name, expires_in_seconds}`. It never supplies or receives a filesystem path. Images have a null playback URL and can be used by explicit save/reveal actions.

Only the authenticated local owner document loader can create a frame, register a backend result, or revoke a frame. Playback GET/HEAD self-authenticates with an exact opaque plugin/frame/handle path. The owner bearer credential never appears in playback URLs or document markup. Other routes retain bearer authentication. The existing exact-origin CORS policy exposes the frame header alongside CSP for desktop and web loaders; it grants no new origins. The common loader adds only this frame's absolute media path and blob playback to media-src; connect-src stays none. Frame bridge messages must come from the current iframe, and asynchronous completions recheck that identity.

Frames expire after 30 minutes and handles after 10 minutes (bounded by frame lifetime). Limits are 128 frames globally, 16 per plugin, 16 handles per frame, and 256 MiB per file. Expiration is checked on every operation and stream chunk; stale entries are reclaimed on the next document/provider access. Document replacement, close, or in-frame reload revokes the frame. Plugin reload/unload revokes every plugin frame. A missing cleanup request therefore remains bounded by expiry and store caps. Source files remain plugin-owned and are never deleted by handle cleanup.

Registration opens the plugin root and every child without following symlinks/reparse points, verifies a regular nonempty file, size, passive MIME and container signature, and sanitizes the display filename with a passive extension. Playback retains that open file and reads in at most 64 KiB blocks with explicit offsets under one cursor lock; it never reopens the path. Gesture consumers use `open_frame_media(plugin, frame, handle)`, which checks exact-frame ownership and repeats the same confined open/format/size validation. Returned paths are for explicit reveal only. File contents remain mutable by the owning plugin; a handle is delivery authority, not a content digest or archival guarantee.

Only single RFC byte ranges are supported. Full, suffix, bounded and open-ended ranges work; multiple, malformed, oversized, overflowing and unsatisfiable ranges return 416 after authorization. HEAD returns the same headers without reading a body. Responses use a finite MIME allowlist, nosniff, no-store and Accept-Ranges. Unknown, foreign and expired playback capabilities produce the same 404 without media metadata.

The native ViewProvider and JS mediaFile export share one descriptor and file model, with parity fixtures. `open_owned_media` reuses validation for host-stamped producer plugins but conveys no Team, workspace or run authority. Durable Blueprint references and authorized cross-plugin handoff belong to the execution layer; they must not persist a frame token or claim that a mutable plugin source is an immutable artifact.

Canonical validation: plugin/service/API lane-check with tests; plugin nextest selectors `media_delivery` and existing code-source fixtures; API nextest `plugin_media_routes` and `web_plugin_routes`; Vitest pluginDocument and PluginView.activation; fmt, file-size/layering/API-effect guards. Worker authored fixtures only; no executions performed.

# Plugin surface tabs

A surface tab is a tab whose content a plugin renders. Domios owns the frame:
the tab's identity, owner, header, lifecycle and restore. The plugin owns what
is inside. Surface tabs sit in the sidebar next to terminals and chats, nested
under the tab that owns them, and render the same way in the desktop app and
the web mirror.

A surface renders in one of two ways. A `view` surface shows the plugin's
sandboxed view (`ui/index.html`), the same page the plugin shows as a panel. A
`stream` surface shows live frames from a core surface runtime, such as the
browser, and the viewer's clicks and keys go back to that runtime.

## Declaring a surface

A plugin declares its surfaces in `plugin.json`:

```json
"capabilities": {
  "view": true,
  "surfaces": [
    { "id": "board", "title": "Board", "renderer": "view", "agentBound": true, "restore": "relaunch" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| `id` | 1-32 lowercase letters, digits or `-`, unique within the plugin |
| `title` | One word without whitespace; it becomes the tab title |
| `renderer` | `view` (the plugin must also declare `capabilities.view`) or `stream` |
| `runtime` | Required for `stream`, refused for `view`: the core surface runtime that renders it. Only `browser` exists |
| `chrome` | Optional, `stream` only: a toolbar spec object core passes to the frontend untouched |
| `agentBound` | Optional. The tab is labelled after its owner, e.g. `Jev's Board` |
| `restore` | Optional: `relaunch` (default), `placeholder` or `none` |
| `agentVerbs` | View only: up to 32 unique lowercase kebab verbs of 1-32 bytes; defaults empty |
| `stateInvalidation` | View only: opt into identity-only state hints; defaults false |
| `icon` | Optional: a Lucide icon name for the tab, lowercase kebab of at most 40 characters (e.g. `globe`); an invalid name is ignored with a warning instead of failing the load. `GET /api/surfaces` carries it on the declared row |

A plugin declares at most 8 surfaces. A manifest that breaks a rule fails to
load, so the plugin never registers a surface it cannot render.

A stream surface needs no view: core branches on the declared `runtime`, never
on the plugin id, and a runtime core does not have refuses the open with
`surface_runtime_unavailable`.

A view surface re-renders on every `restore` value, because a view keeps no
live state of its own. A stream surface with `relaunch` reopens where it was:
the browser runtime reloads its last http(s) or file page in the same profile,
falling back to the clean profile when that profile is gone. `placeholder` and
`none` keep the tab and start the runtime fresh.

The view page receives `surface`, `instance` and `tab` through `ct.surface`
and talks to the plugin through `ct.invoke`, exactly like
the panel view. One plugin view can serve several surfaces by reading
`surface`, and several open copies of one surface by reading `instance`.

### Host actions from a view

A view can ask the host to act on the user's behalf through `ct.host`, but only
for the actions its manifest declares in `capabilities.viewHostActions`
(`copyText`, `saveAs`, `reveal`; it requires `view`):

- `ct.host.copyText(text)` puts plain text on the clipboard.
- `ct.host.saveAs(mediaHandle, suggestedName)` saves one of the plugin's own
  media files: the desktop app asks where with the system save dialog, the web
  mirror downloads it.
- `ct.host.reveal(mediaHandle)` shows that file in the system file manager. The
  web mirror refuses it.

Each call resolves to `{ ok: true }` or `{ ok: false, code, reason }` and never
throws. `denied` means there was no user gesture, the action is not declared,
the user cancelled, or the handle does not belong to this frame;
`unavailable` means the host cannot act here; `invalid` means a malformed
argument. Call them from a click or key handler. The host's check is a
recent-activation heuristic, not proof that one fresh click asked for one
effect: copyText and reveal act only when the view is shown, its frame holds
focus and the app had user activation within the browser's short activation
window, all observed by the app itself. A view that is hidden or does not hold
focus is refused. One call runs at a time per frame, and calls are rate-limited
to one effect per second (`denied` / `busy`); the limit bounds repeats, it does
not prove a new gesture. saveAs gets its real per-intent confirmation from the
system save dialog (on the web mirror, the browser's download). Every copy shows
a "Copied from <plugin>" notice that the plugin cannot hide. A frame hidden,
closed, reloaded, navigated or replaced while a call is pending gets `denied` /
`stale`, and nothing happens. `ct.host.availability()` resolves to
`{ copyText, saveAs, reveal }` booleans saying what this app can perform here
(the web mirror cannot reveal; a page without a clipboard cannot copy). Use it
to hide an action, not to probe one; it grants nothing, and every call is still
checked. `denied` with `media_expired` means this frame's access to the file
lapsed, not that the file is gone: reopen the result to get a fresh handle.
A media handle is the opaque handle
the host issued to this frame; a reloaded frame gets new handles. The view never
sees or sends a file path.

## Opening, listing and closing

```bash
domios surface list
domios surface open dash:board
domios surface open dash:board --owner <TAB>
domios surface close --tab <TAB>
```

- `surface list` shows the surfaces enabled plugins declare and the surface
  tabs that are open, with their owners. `--json` returns `declared` and `open`.
- `surface open <plugin_id>:<surface_id>` checks that the plugin is installed,
  enabled, declares that surface and can render it (a registered view, or the
  declared stream runtime), then creates the tab and prints its id.
- The owner is `--owner`, otherwise the calling tab when it is an agent tab.
  A plain shell caller opens an ownerless surface. A surface cannot own another
  surface.
- The tab nests under its owner (`parent_tab_id`), opens in the owner's
  workspace and joins the owner's Team through the same membership check as
  `tab new`, so a Team without a live Orchestrator refuses the open. Closing
  the Team closes the surface.
- The tab title is the surface title. The tab header and the sidebar show
  `{Owner}'s {Title}` when the surface is `agentBound` or was opened with
  `--title-from-owner`; the label follows the owner if it is renamed.
- `surface close --tab <TAB>` closes a surface tab and refuses any other tab,
  so it can never close an agent. The tab menu, the header close button and
  `domios tab close` close it too.

## Surface tabs take no text

A surface has no terminal and no agent. Every text path refuses it with a typed
code instead of starting a shell:

- `domios send`, the `/send` and chat-send routes, and agent-to-agent
  delivery return `surface_no_input`.
- `domios tab get-text` and output reads return `surface_no_text`.

Act on a surface through its plugin's verbs (`domios plugin --help` lists
installed plugins; each plugin documents its own verbs).

## Lifecycle

- The tab survives restarts and desk restore with its plugin, surface and
  instance ids.
- When the owner tab closes, by any path, its surfaces close with it. Other
  children of the owner are detached as before.
- When the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, the tab stays but its view can
  no longer reach the plugin; close it or re-enable the plugin.
- A stream surface's runtime starts on first use (a viewer connecting or an
  agent verb) and is disposed when the tab closes by any path: `surface close`,
  the owner closing, the workspace closing or the Team closing. The browser
  runtime then closes its Chromium.

## Stream surfaces

A viewer and the agent who owns the surface drive the same runtime instance.
The viewer uses the two routes below; the owner agent uses its plugin's verbs.

### The browser

The `browser` plugin declares `browser:browser`, a stream surface on the
`browser` runtime. Its owner agent drives it with the plugin verbs
(`domios plugin browser <verb>`); the plugin's `help` verb prints the
full guide. The verbs act only on the calling agent's own browser, and
`open` creates it when the agent has none. When the user points at an element
and sends a question, change or bug, the owner agent receives it as a Domios
notice; a bare shell owner is refused, and `inbox` returns what was not
delivered or read.

### Plugin access

A plugin calls `host.surface.call(verb, argsJson)` inside `onAgentCommand`,
with the `surfaces` permission. The first declared stream or view with nonempty
`agentVerbs` is selected. The result is JSON text `{result:string}` or `{error:string}`.
Arguments are a word array or `{args,of}`, at most 32768 UTF-8 bytes. `of` resolves
an agent id/title only inside the caller's workspace; mesh-controlled callers
cannot use it. Own `open` creates the attachment; another agent may drive an
already-open attachment but cannot open or close it. Activity contains only the
sanitized verb and acting agent label, never arguments.

For a view, declared verbs call the synchronous export
`onSurfaceCall(context, verb, args): string`. The host supplies
`context = {surface,instance,tab,owner,actor,actorLabel}`. Owner and actor are tab
ids; actorLabel is sanitized display text. Arguments cannot override this context.
`open`/`close` remain host lifecycle verbs; declaring `open` also calls the export
after opening. An undeclared view verb refuses before dispatch. Missing handlers,
exceptions and oversized results return an error. A result does not imply a remote
job finished; keep job state and cancellation support in the plugin.

With `stateInvalidation:true`, backend exports may call
`host.surface.invalidate({surface,instance,tab})` and receive `{ok:true}` or `{error}`.
The host stamps the plugin id and emits `surface-state-invalidated` only for that
plugin's exact live view instance. The input is strict, at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes;
no custom event payload is accepted. Closed, replaced or unloaded instances refuse.
The exact document receives a hint without reload or polling. Subscribe through
`ct.onSurfaceStateChanged(callback)`; its return value unsubscribes. Refetch through
`ct.invoke`, also on initial mount; hints carry no state or delivery guarantee.
Frame readiness supplies a catch-up hint. Reopening never refreshes the old instance.

Stream verbs continue through their core runtime. Stream `annotate` delivers an
element card to the surface owner, signed by the caller.

## REST

| Method | Path | Body | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/surfaces` | — | `{ declared: [...], open: [...] }` |
| POST | `/api/surfaces/open` | `{ target, owner_tab_id?, caller_tab_id?, workspace_id?, title_from_owner? }` | The opened tab row |
| POST | `/api/surfaces/close` | `{ tab_id, caller_tab_id? }` | `{ tab_id, warnings }` |

| GET | `/api/surfaces/{tab_id}/stream?w=&h=&dpr=` | — | SSE stream of a stream surface |
| POST | `/api/surfaces/{tab_id}/call` | `{ method, args }` | `{ result }` or `{ error }` |

`target` is `<plugin_id>:<surface_id>`. With an owner, `workspace_id` must be
the owner's workspace. Declared rows carry `runtime` and `chrome` for stream
surfaces.

`stream` takes the viewer's CSS size and DPR and applies it before the first
frame. It sends `state` (`{ owner, title, url, activity, needsHuman, profile,
profiles }`) on connect and on every change, `frame` (`{ data, metadata }`,
`data` a base64 JPEG, latest-wins and paced by core; the client never acks)
and `notice` (`{ text, tone? }`). The stream counts as a viewer while it is
open; the last viewer leaving stops the frames. Authenticate with the
`Authorization` header, as with every other route.

`call` methods: `resize { width, height, dpr }`, `input { kind: click | wheel
| text | key, x?, y?, deltaY?, text?, key?, shift?, ctrl?, alt?, meta? }`,
`nav { action: goto | back | forward | reload, target? }`, `screenshot { full? }`
→ `{ base64, path }` (a PNG saved in the owner's pad, or the data dir without
one), `profiles.list` and `profiles.use { name }` (`""` or `clean` is the clean
profile) → `{ current, profiles }`, `grab.hover { x, y }`, `grab.cancel`,
`grab.select { x, y }` → `{ id, label, target }` and `grab.send { id, comment,
intent: question | change | bug }` → `{ markdown, delivered }`, `snip.capture
{ x, y, w, h }` (document CSS px) → `{ id, width, height, thumbnail }` (kept in
memory, nothing written), `snip.cancel { id }` and `snip.send { id, comment,
image? }` → `{ markdown, delivered }` (with `image`, the PNG is saved in the
owner's pad and attached).

Refusals carry `{ ok: false, error: { code, message } }`:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `invalid_surface_target` | `target` is not `<plugin_id>:<surface_id>` |
| `surface_plugin_unavailable` | The plugin is not installed and enabled with a view |
| `surface_not_declared` | The plugin declares no such surface |
| `surface_view_unavailable` | The plugin's view is not registered |
| `surface_owner_not_found` | The named owner tab does not exist |
| `surface_owner_is_surface` | The owner is itself a surface tab |
| `surface_workspace_mismatch` | `workspace_id` differs from the owner's workspace |
| `not_a_surface` | `surface close` named a tab that is not a surface |
| `not_a_stream_surface` | `stream` or `call` named a tab that is not a stream surface (HTTP 409) |
| `surface_runtime_unavailable` | The declared stream runtime is not registered in core (HTTP 409) |

# Blueprints

Named binds accept only json/text producers; media ports in named binds are not supported yet.

Recall saved solutions before authoring; reuse a match or built-in. Blueprints use `schema_version: 2` and one typed graph. Older formats refuse; stored v1 graphs/solutions are deleted without conversion, preserving other memory/workspaces.

```bash
domios blueprint new --intent "watch CI and report failures" --json
domios blueprint recipe
domios blueprint new http-health > health.yaml
domios blueprint check health.yaml --set url=https://example.com/health
domios blueprint apply health.yaml --set url=https://example.com/health --dry-run
domios blueprint apply health.yaml --set url=https://example.com/health
```

`new <recipe|watch|pipeline|command>` prints YAML. `check`/`apply` accept recipes, filenames or stdin (`-`); `create` aliases `apply`. Named scaffolds, schema and call-free checks work offline. `new --intent` recall and typed-call checking use live Team/workspace admission; applying additionally checks live targets and installed capabilities. An offer never starts a graph.

## Repository discovery and human review

From the repository root, read `.domios/blueprints/` without applying:

```bash
domios blueprint project list --json
domios blueprint project show .domios/blueprints/health.yaml --json
```

Discovery returns path/name/intent. Names must match file stems; linked/escaping paths, duplicate stems across extensions and files over 64 KiB refuse. Listing, viewing and repository edits never execute or approve graphs; execution requires separate repository trust approval.

The Jobs view shares repository discovery and typed read-only canvases. A call exposes its pinned id/hash, inputs, result and body; a selected run shows its own journal, nested stops and callee paths. Trigger/Result follow `$run`/`$result` evidence. Held nodes show their recorded reason. Plan-locked owners hold with `plan_limit_locked`: apply/edit/run refuse; delete/export remain; unlock resumes the cursor, while watches baseline before later changes. Semantic diff compares retained versions; parameter fields expose `--set` without submission.

## Native v2 documents

```yaml
schema_version: 2
kind: pipeline
name: Service health
note: Probe a service and report its health
intent: watch an HTTP endpoint for outages
owner: team
inputs:
  url: {type: string, description: Service health endpoint}
trigger:
  type: schedule
  every: {lit: 1m}
steps:
  - id: health
    uses: http
    with:
      url: {input: url}
      timeout_ms: {lit: 3000}
    routes: {up: '@stop', down: '@stop', failed: '@stop'}
result: {to: notify}
```

Metadata includes `name`, a printable `note` of at most 200 characters, optional `intent` and `anchors`, typed `inputs` and named port `types`. `kind` is `pipeline` or `watch`. Pipeline ownership is `team` or `tab`; a watch remains scoped to its creator and caller Team. Nodes have stable, unique `id` values; array order fixes execution order. Routes name a later node, `@next` or `@stop`. Use `routes`, never `on`.

Values in `with`, `run`, timing fields and call arguments have exactly one form:

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `{lit: value}` | Author-fixed JSON data or executable text |
| `{input: name}` | An author input supplied before apply |
| `{bind: node.out.field}` | Runtime data from a preceding node |

Domios does not evaluate expressions or expand executable templates. A `run` input supplies the entire author-fixed shell command line, rather than inserting runtime data into a command. `name: '{{name}}'` may refer to one whole string input. Domios passes command text unchanged to the shell, which applies its own quoting and expansion. Non-string `--set key=value` values use JSON syntax. Unknown, duplicate or missing input assignments refuse.

Ports use the restricted JSON Schema fields `type`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `enum`, `items`, `maxLength` and `x-media`, or `{$ref: TypeName}`. Inputs additionally support `default` and `description`. Typed `in`/`out`, `bind`, capability `caps`, code metadata, local `imports`, inline `blueprints` and pipeline `other` handlers are represented in the document and its canonical graph/diff projections.

## Execution support

Admission lowers a v2 document to the runtime representation or returns an explicit unsupported diagnostic before effects. Code and call nodes execute through the shared typed runtime. Runtime data binds resolve retained outputs as data. Lowering refuses any unsupported node or contract before effects; pipeline `other` handlers remain unavailable. `domios-cli` capability is unavailable.

Supported pipeline nodes are `code`, fixed `run` commands and `uses: http`, `github`, `ask`, `filter`, `convert` and `agent`. Parameters are explicit value forms. `ask` declares its `buckets` on the node. HTTP outcomes are `up`, `down`, `failed`; GitHub outcomes depend on `resource`; filters may declare a bucket. Commands, conversion and agent tasks return `done` or `failed`. Unspecified failure routes stop; other unspecified outcomes continue. Inputs and outputs must agree with the supported media chain. `result.to` accepts `owner`, `team`, `notify` or `tab:<id>`; offline checking refuses any other target. With the default `owner: team`, `owner` and `team` deliver to the Team Orchestrator's inbox in the Blueprint's workspace; with `owner: tab`, `owner` delivers to the applying tab.

`run` is a shell command line, not argv; runtime values arrive in its stdin envelope. `bind: {in: prior.out}` passes one value unchanged. Code/command named ports (`bind: {a: first.out, b: second.out}`) pass `{a: <first value>, b: <second value>}` to Python/TS `main(value)` or command envelope `value`. A closed object schema is inferred when `in` is omitted; declared object schemas are checked per port. Use up to 32 nonempty port names, at most 64 bytes without dots; never mix them with `in`. All binds, including call arguments, require data dominance: every path to the consumer must execute its producer, including after merges. Positioned `D1` names the producer and a skipping branch path. Shell details/example: `domios docs BLUEPRINT-AUTHORING`.

Command steps default to a 10-second runtime on every platform. Override it on the node with `timeout: {lit: 30s}` (also accepts an author input). The timeout must be positive and at most 60 seconds; invalid values receive a positioned checker diagnostic. For example:

```yaml
- id: inspect
  run: {lit: git status --short}
  timeout: {lit: 30s}
```

Watcher probes also default to 10 seconds on every platform. Each watcher runs concurrently, so a slow probe delays its own verdict while the scheduler and other watchers continue. Command and probe runtime budgets start when the direct child's spawn call returns, excluding its exec authorization delay. Runtime is followed by bounded cleanup of up to 500 ms (one quarter of a shorter budget): the total is runtime plus that reserve, capped by the caller's remaining run deadline. A shorter caller deadline reserves cleanup within that total and may interrupt execution earlier; expiry produces a typed `Deadline`.

A schedule trigger has `every: {lit: 20s}`. Input triggers have a media `kind` and a `source` literal containing `text`, an absolute `file` path or an HTTP(S) `url`; a string source denotes text.

A `text` trigger delivers a **string**: `{text: "7"}` reaches the first node as the string `"7"`, never the integer 7. The text is parsed as JSON only when the first node's `in` schema rejects a string and the parsed value satisfies that schema (`in: {type: integer}` with `"7"` delivers 7; `in: {type: object, ...}` with `{"n":7}` delivers the object). With no `in` schema the node receives the string. To pass structured data, declare the object schema on the first node's `in` or parse the string in code. A mismatch stops the node with `contract_violation`; its journal summary and `show` name the expected schema and the received media and value (clipped), for example `node stopped: contract_violation: input expected {"type":"integer"} got text "seven"`. Event triggers name an installed capability kind and explicit parameters. Runtime availability is checked at apply.

## Webhook triggers and threat model

Use `trigger: {type: webhook, schema: {type: object}}` with optional `schema`. POST delivers parsed JSON; `"7"` stays a string. Caps: HTTP 1 MiB, depth 32, typed stdin 32 KiB. Invalid/oversized inputs refuse before execution.

```bash
domios blueprint webhook enable <id> --reveal
domios blueprint webhook show-url <id>
domios blueprint webhook rotate <id> --reveal
domios blueprint webhook disable <id>
```

Enable generates a secret-store credential; enabling twice refuses. Rotate immediately invalidates the old secret; disable removes it. Enable/rotate reveal the new secret once to stdout only with `--reveal`.

POST `application/json` to `/api/blueprints/<id>/webhook` with `Authorization: Bearer <secret>` or `X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256>` over the raw body using that secret. The daemon token is refused. Optional `X-Webhook-Timestamp` is Unix seconds: sign `<timestamp>.<raw body>` instead; tolerance is five minutes. Raw GitHub signatures have no timestamp protection.

`X-Delivery-Id` or `X-GitHub-Delivery` deduplicates for ten minutes and returns the original run ID. IDs are 1–128 printable ASCII bytes; retention caps at 256 per graph/4096 globally. Counters reset on restart. Delivery headers are unsigned; timestamps bound replay. Limits: 30 admissions/graph/minute, 120 attempts globally/minute, eight active graph runs; busy admission returns 409.

Payloads never choose executable text or paths: commands receive JSON stdin, code typed values. Author code retains OS permissions and must never splice data into shell source. Auth uses constant-time comparison; secrets stay out of URLs/logs/errors/run records. Runs retain an auth audit row and use the existing executor. Inactive/missing hooks return 404. Hooks share API loopback/Tailnet listeners; public callers need a TLS tunnel without credential logging.

## Code nodes

`code.lang` is `python` or `ts` (`typescript` is refused). `shell` parses but is not runnable: a `code` body must declare `main`, so shell text belongs in a fixed `run` command step. Limits sit under the code block (`code: {lang: python, src: ..., limits: {wall_ms: 3000, output_bytes: 32768}}`); a node-level `limits` is also accepted. Code nodes run in a throwaway temporary working directory, while command and probe steps run in the Blueprint cwd. Python bodies define `def main(value):` and return a JSON value. TypeScript bodies define `export default function main(value)` (optionally async). A fixed per-language harness reads the bounded input envelope, calls `main` with its `value`, and writes the result with the node’s output media and schema. Text uses a string `value` and an empty `text` field, so it is carried once. Author prints go to stderr. Raw envelope scripts are unsupported.

```yaml
- id: swatch
  code: {lang: python, src: 'def main(value): return "linen"'}
  out: {type: string}
- id: caption
  code: {lang: python, src: 'def main(value): return value.upper()'}
  bind: {in: swatch.out}
  in: {type: string}
  out: {type: string}
```

`code.src` is bounded to 16 KiB. Alternatively, `code.file` names a relative regular file beneath the directory of the Blueprint file that declares it. Absolute paths, parent traversal, symlinks and Windows junctions or other reparse points at any component refuse with `contract_violation`, and the resolved file must stay inside that directory; the same reader serves apply and runtime. Apply freezes its bounded bytes into `code.src` before persisting the graph. Later file edits do not change the stored body. Canonical nodes and execution summaries carry `body_sha256`. Runtime refuses unsealed `code.file` and missing `main`.

Python and TypeScript code nodes run as ordinary child processes on macOS, Linux and Windows, using Python or Node from the filtered PATH. Python uses the fixed `main(value)` harness; TypeScript uses Node's type stripping and the fixed exported `main(value)` harness.

Blueprint code and command steps run with the user's own permissions, like an agent in a tab, without Domios credentials in their environment. They can access the user's files, network and subprocesses, including Domios data directories and the instance credentials stored there. Code nodes and command steps both run in the Blueprint's cwd and keep the user's identity, home and temp variables (`USERNAME`, `USERPROFILE`, `HOMEDRIVE`, `HOMEPATH`, `TEMP`, `TMP`, `APPDATA`, `LOCALAPPDATA` on Windows; `HOME`, `USER`, `LOGNAME`, `TMPDIR` elsewhere); `CODETERM*`/`DOMIOS*` variables and other credentials are dropped. Foreign Blueprints are gated by folder trust (1.15.4); inspect their code and commands before granting trust.

`wall_ms` defaults to 3000 for code; `output_bytes` defaults to 32768 and bounds combined stdout/stderr during capture. There is **no default `mem_mb`**. An explicit code memory cap uses `RLIMIT_AS` on Linux and the existing process Job's memory limit on Windows. On macOS, the checker emits the positioned warning `mem_mb not enforced on this OS`; checking, admission and execution continue with deadline and output limits. Memory budgets on other nodes, output budgets on HTTP/agent nodes and watch limits refuse. Command/GitHub output budgets and pipeline wall deadlines remain enforced.

Ordinary exceptions and non-zero code exits produce routable `failed`, reason `code_failed`, with a bounded, redacted stderr tail. Invalid contracts, deadlines and exhausted output budgets stop before routing further effects.

The stdin envelope remains bounded to 32 KiB. Plain text of 20 KiB passes intact. Oversized serialized payloads become an explicit JSON truncation value with `type: truncated`, `truncated: true`, `total_bytes`, `limit_bytes` and a bounded UTF-8 `prefix`. Typed contracts validate that delivered value and may refuse a truncation marker that violates their schema.

Command steps and watcher probes preserve the daemon's inherited PATH order, remove the explicitly configured Domios CLI directories, and append missing default tool directories. Other inherited variables are excluded; children receive `LANG` and, on Windows, `SystemRoot`, `PATHEXT` for tool-name resolution and a `COMSPEC` pointing to the system `cmd.exe` for batch files.

## Watches and effects

```yaml
schema_version: 2
kind: watch
name: Build result
note: Notify when the build passes
steps:
  - id: source
    uses: probe
    with: {command: {lit: echo passed}}
    every: {lit: 20s}
    timeout: {lit: 1h}
  - id: decide
    uses: ask
    with: {question: {lit: Did the build pass?}}
    buckets: [waiting, passed]
    matches: {passed: {lit: '(?m)^passed\r?$'}}
    until: passed
    routes: {waiting: '@stop', passed: alert}
  - id: alert
    uses: notify
```

A watch starts with one source and an `ask` decision. Sources are `probe` with a fixed `command`, `observe` with `kind` (`tab` or `cron_run`) and `id`, or `input` with a media `kind` and `text`, absolute `file` or `url`. An input source can request `convert_to` and `convert_timeout_ms`. Terminal observations use `uses: terminal` with tab binding, `pattern` and/or `idle_ms`.

Source `every` defaults to 20 seconds and is at least 10 seconds. Durations use `s`, `m`, `h`, `d` or combinations, bounded to 366 days. `timeout`, `paused` and `session` belong on the source. The decision owns `matches`, `until`, `rearm_on_change`, `model_classification` and `escalation_timeout_ms`. Keep waiting silent by routing it to `@stop`; this ends that watch's action chain without stopping future observations.

Effects are nodes: `notify`, `send`, `cron`, `blueprint`, `respond_prompt`, `escalate` and `stop`. Targeted effects use `with: {target: {lit: ...}}`; a `done` route can chain later effects. An `other` route may reach notify/escalate nodes and requires a positive escalation timeout on the decision. Only unknown cases escalate. Prompt-response effects request the provider-declared safe path; they do not select keys or options. Commands and targets stay author-fixed and scope-bound. Claims persist before effects, and uncertain delivery never authorizes replay.

## Checking, apply and sharing

```bash
domios blueprint schema > blueprint.schema.json
domios blueprint check health.yaml --set url=https://example.com/health --json --explain
domios blueprint check health.yaml --fix
domios blueprint check health.yaml --fix --write
domios blueprint export <id> --out shared.yaml
domios blueprint import shared.yaml --scope general --set command="echo ready"
domios blueprint update <id> --expect-version 3 --from-file health-bound.yaml --dry-run
domios blueprint show <id>
domios blueprint history <id>
domios blueprint log <id>
```

Schema/parser share one model; offline check and live apply/import/update share one checker. Diagnostics retain rule/atom IDs, file/line/column/field, severity, message, hint, premises and proof trees. Dependent findings fold under their root. `--explain` lists causal premises under `CAUSED BY` and other premises under `GIVEN`; unpositioned live errors name the field. JSON preserves structure. Invalid files exit 2; unsupported constructs refuse. `apply --dry-run` also checks live Team scope and capabilities.

`--fix` previews only candidates passing checking/lowering with supplied `--set`; `--write` writes them. Repairs declare unambiguous inputs, warn when normalizing sub-10s timing, or route watch `other` to creator escalation. Ambiguous, unresolved, executable/authority and pipeline-escalation repairs refuse unchanged. R13 compares scoped saved/live graphs, ignoring descriptive metadata. Exact/generalized twins match content; structural twins share WL shape and all code, parameters, sources and defaults. Different code/literals remain distinct; missing embeddings report unavailable comparisons.

Import accepts `--scope general`, `workspace:<id>` or `team:<id>` only for a member of that scope; omission uses the caller's scope. Team-less imports are tab-owned, live with their creator and report to it. Team ownership/delivery and callable reuse require a real Team.

An exact name identifies a graph in its Team/workspace. Built-in names stay stable when bindings change; apply retargets that name. Use an explicit `name` input when distinct identities are required. Applying unchanged running definitions returns `unchanged`; applying a stopped graph reactivates the same ID. Watch lifetime and initial pause settings cannot change through apply. A watch and pipeline cannot replace one another under the same name.

Export generalizes sensitive commands, source data and local targets into described required inputs, excluding runtime state and history. Import uses the same v2 admission and starts stopped unless `--start` is passed. `update --from-file` accepts a native v2 document with its required inputs already bound or defaulted; it enforces the expected version and optional cause. Internal history JSON is not an authoring format. Stopped graphs retain their history for 30 minutes before cleanup.

## Recall before authoring

`blueprint new --intent` returns the exact-intent scaffold and three compact scoped recall cards (`--limit`: 1..20). JSON includes `scaffold`, `yaml`, `cards`, `recall` and `unavailable`. Cards expose stable `mem:`/`catalog:` IDs, hashes, provenance, scores, WHY, port schemas and node counts, never executable bodies; open one with `blueprint show <card-id>`. Ranked recall uses current intent vectors, descriptions and enrichment for saved solutions and compatible built-ins after Team/workspace scoping. Missing vectors report degraded/pending status without lexical fallback; incompatible catalogue contracts report unavailable.

Reuse a fitting card by a typed `call`; require the complete purpose and port contract to fit. Scores alone do not prove fit; author from scratch when none fits. Call checking returns the sealed native definition, including its `{id, hash}` pins and immutable dependencies; save that returned definition before apply. Missing revisions refuse and retained pins never silently rebind.

Literal call arguments must satisfy the complete callee schema. Each array item is checked independently, allowing differing values and optional fields; empty arrays satisfy `items`. Required fields, enums, `maxLength` and `additionalProperties` apply to each item. `catalog:checks-fan-in` accepts mixed pass/fail objects or `checks: []`.

## Saved solutions

```bash
domios blueprint keep <id> --when "Watch CI and report failing jobs early" --tag ci --tag github --when "tell me when a pull request goes red" --when "ping me once a check fails"
domios blueprint apply memory:<recipe-id> --set key=value
```

Only the Team Orchestrator keeps solutions. Supply 1–5 intents, preferably 3–5 distinct requests. Generalization retains required typed inputs and removes instance defaults. Recall preserves server ranking, per-intent vectors, semantic canon, structural signatures, enrichment provenance and bounded variant merging. Saves retain their own entry and report cap-archived IDs; unavailable workers leave enrichment pending.

Callable names must describe their contents. Keeping different contents under an existing name in the same scope refuses with `blueprint_name_conflict` and suggests a purpose-based name. Revise an existing solution by ID. Automatic callable merges require matching executable contents and agreeing purposes; distant purpose vectors never merge. Without purpose vectors, only identical purpose text can merge. Presentation-only title and note changes do not change executable identity. Retained pins continue to use their immutable revisions.

Recipe purposes/inputs: `domios docs BLUEPRINT-RECIPES`.

A callable declares a schema object in `result.type`, for example `result: {type: {type: integer}, from: add.out}`; bare type names refuse.

Save a triggerless typed callable without scheduling it:

```bash
domios blueprint keep --file increment.yaml --when "Increment a typed counter" --tag data-transform
domios blueprint show mem:<solution-id> --json
```

Keep returns typed inputs and a stable `mem:` ID/hash for `call.ref`. Relative imports freeze a scoped transitive closure; escaping or linked paths refuse. Export preserves pins; archived heads refuse new pins, existing pins never rebind, and missing bytes refuse execution. `show` exposes pinned bodies, bounded nested results and stops; unavailable history is explicit. Call checks share apply admission and preserve signatures without scheduling. `keep --file` saves callables; `apply` schedules graphs; `check --fix` refuses calls.

Callable `other` handlers are refused at check time; move failure handling to the caller. Inside callees, notify/send/cron/escalate use caller scope and the shared executor claim. Blueprint activation, stop and prompt-response effects require scheduler custody and are refused at check time inside calls; put those effects in the caller.

The simulation harness is internal and has no CLI verb. It records bounded delivery provenance in memory with zero delivery and no real run journal. Process, code, agent, HTTP and conversion nodes refuse before launch; pure filters and calls share the normal budget and port checks.

Restored PTY results wait in a durable outbox for the exact saved provider/session's authenticated launch, with a fixed 24-hour TTL and original run ID/timestamp. Closed/changed/failed/expired recipients produce an idempotent delivery-ID failure receipt and status event; live producers also receive a failure notification. Interrupted settlement re-emits status; edited receipts remain. Uncertain writes never replay. Chat backends retain the existing reopen path and report failures, but lack this durable hold.

R10 and environment scrubbing prevent accidents, not hostile code. R10 joins split literals and refuses whole words `domios`/`codeterm`, tokens prefixed `DOMIOS_`/`CODETERM_` with `ambient_authority`; domios-cli capabilities also refuse. Obfuscation can pass. Children scrub instance credentials/private CLI paths and shadow CLI names with private PATH-first deny stubs, retaining shared paths such as `/usr/bin`. HOME/APPDATA and absolute executables remain available under user authority. Unavailable R13 comparisons never claim PASS.

# Integration configuration

Configuration keys for messaging, hooks, transcription, and secret-backed integrations.

## Integrations

External service integrations are configured under `[integrations]`.

### Telegram Bridge

Connect a Telegram bot to the General Agent. Messages are routed bidirectionally:
- **Inbound** (Telegram to Agent): Messages arrive as `[Telegram: user_id] text` in the PTY. Rapid messages within 300ms are debounced into a single delivery. A typing indicator is sent on every inbound message.
- **Outbound** (Agent to Telegram): The agent sends replies via CLI: `domios bridge send --to USER_ID --service telegram "text"`. Without `--append`, always sends a new message. Use `--append` to concatenate text to the previous message (auto-inserts `\n\n` paragraph break, edits in-place within 60s window). Works from any tab, not just the General Agent.

```toml
[integrations]
telegram_enabled = false
telegram_allowed_users = []     # Telegram user IDs as strings, empty = allow all
```

**Setup:**
1. Create a bot via @BotFather on Telegram, get the token
2. Save token to `~/.domios/secrets/telegram.token`
3. Enable: `domios config set integrations.telegram_enabled true`
4. Optionally restrict users: `domios config set integrations.telegram_allowed_users '["123456789"]'`
5. Restart Domios (hot-reload not yet supported)

Connected services are shown as icons next to the tab title in the sidebar (`connected_services` field on the tab object).

Settings UI: Settings > General > Messengers (Telegram bot bridge toggle + allowed users list).

### Discord (coming soon)

```toml
discord_enabled = false
discord_allowed_users = []
```

### Webhooks (integration bridge)

```toml
webhook_enabled = false
webhook_port = 7687
```

### Pre-forward text hooks (since v1.2.0)

Generic intercept point for inbound bridge messages BEFORE they reach the General Agent tab. An external daemon receives the message via HTTP and decides one of three outcomes: forward unchanged, replace (daemon already responded — bridge skips the tab), or annotate with metadata that the agent can act on.

Same shape as `voice_transcribe` (health-cache + timeout + fallback) but routed for text/command messages.

```toml
[integrations.text_hooks]
enabled = false
daemon_url = "http://127.0.0.1:7892"
timeout_ms = 2000
health_check_ttl_secs = 60
fallback_on_error = "forward"      # "forward" | "drop"
```

**Daemon protocol:**

```
GET  /healthz                      → 200 "ok"

POST /pre_forward
Body: {
  "text":         "turn on the lights downstairs",
  "channel":      "telegram",
  "user_id":      "123456789",
  "msg_id":       "12345",
  "tab_id":      "<target tab>",
  "attachments":  [{"kind": "voice", "path": "/tmp/...", "filename": "..."}]
}

Response (one of):
  {"action": "forward"}                            // standard pass-through
  {"action": "replace",
   "respond": [
     {"channel": "telegram", "to": "123456789",
      "text": "done — lights are on downstairs"}
   ]}                                              // bridge sends reply, skips GA
  {"action": "forward_with_metadata",
   "metadata": {"router_label": "light_cmd",
                "extracted_action": "lights.sh downstairs on"}}
                                                   // GA gets text + [Hook metadata: …] line
```

**Use cases:**

- **Trivial command shortcut** — regex first, then Groq llama-3.1-8b (~65ms): 80%+ of TG commands resolved in <100ms instead of 2-5s Claude latency, no token burn.
- **FAQ/auto-reply** — embedding match against curated answers + cached weather/time API.
- **Rate-limit / debounce** — drop duplicates within an N-second window without touching agent prompts.
- **Channel routing** — annotate mesh-relay pings as routine in metadata so GA logs them and moves on.

**Safety / guarantees:**

- Bridge does NOT execute user code. Daemon is a separate process the user runs (parallel to `voice-transcribe`); bridge just talks HTTP.
- Health-cache TTL prevents pummeling a known-down daemon during inbound bursts.
- `fallback_on_error = "forward"` (default) means the message reaches GA when the hook is unreachable, broken, or times out — fail-open. `"drop"` is fail-closed (silence on hook error).
- For `replace`, only `channel: "telegram"` is wired today. Mesh / Discord routes will be added when those bridges land replies.
- The hook only sees `service`-prefixed messages — relayed mesh /send and webhook events bypass it for now (they take a different inject path).

**Setup:**

1. Run a daemon listening on `daemon_url` that handles `GET /healthz` and `POST /pre_forward`.
2. `domios config set integrations.text_hooks.enabled true`
3. `domios config set integrations.text_hooks.daemon_url http://127.0.0.1:7892` (or wherever your daemon listens)
4. Restart bridge (`domios bridge restart`) — picks up the new config.

### Graph nodes (plugin declarations)

A plugin contributes graph nodes through `capabilities.graphNodes` in its manifest: media `converters` and typed `eventSources`. Both lists are optional, and a declared block must name at least one node.

```json
"capabilities": {
  "graphNodes": {
    "converters": [{ "from": "audio", "to": "text" }],
    "eventSources": [{
      "kind": "telegram.message",
      "title": "Telegram: new message",
      "params":  { "type": "object", "properties": { "chat_id": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 128 } }, "required": ["chat_id"] },
      "payload": { "type": "object", "properties": { "text": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 16384 } }, "required": ["text"] }
    }]
  }
}
```

- **converters** declare which media kinds (`text`, `audio`, `video`, `image`) the plugin turns into which (`from` differs from `to`, at most 16). The plugin exports `convert(request)` returning `{ text }`, `{ path }` (a file inside the request's `outputDir`), or `{ error }`. The host chains conversion steps across plugins from the declarations alone, so a plan never depends on which plugin serves a step. A `transcriber` capability is registered as `audio -> text` automatically.
- **eventSources** declare up to 16 event kinds per plugin (`^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*(\.[a-z][a-z0-9_]*)+$`, at most 64 bytes, unique per plugin) with a 1-128 byte title and typed `params`/`payload` schemas. The schema subset is an object of scalar or one-level scalar-array properties (at most 32; `maxLength` <= 65536, `maxItems` <= 256) with optional `description` and `enum`; `$ref`, combinators (`oneOf`/`anyOf`), `patternProperties` and nested objects are refused at parse.
### Model endpoints and presets

`domios model-provider` routes to the installed provider declaring model configuration support. In the app, each such harness's plugin page has a **Custom model endpoints** section with the same operations plus edit and model discovery: a typed key is saved to the secret store (masked, never shown again), or a saved secret is copied into the endpoint's owned slot. The HTTP endpoint `POST /api/model-providers` accepts `?provider=<id>` to address one harness.

Endpoint ids must differ from every installed agent harness id; creation refuses a collision with `harness_id_collision` before saving configuration or credentials. Configured endpoint models appear in `agent models <harness>` even when live discovery fails. Select one with `agent spawn <harness> --model <endpoint>/<model>`; its model is validated against that endpoint's configured models.

```bash
domios model-provider add --name local --kind openai-compatible --base-url http://localhost:1234/v1 --secret local-key --model model-id
domios model-provider list
domios model-provider test --name local
domios model-provider remove --name local
domios model-provider preset add --name demo --model local/model-id --prompt "Review the task" --temperature 0.2 --top-p 0.9 --steps 12
domios model-provider preset list
domios agent spawn opencode --preset demo
domios model-provider preset remove --name demo
```

For `add`, pipe the key from a secure source on stdin; `--secret` is a name, never the value. Repeat `--model` for several models, or omit it to discover models through a connection test. Kinds are `openai-compatible` and `anthropic`. The key lives in the Domios secret store and is injected into the launch environment; OpenCode config contains only `{env:NAME}` references. Endpoint removal deletes only the Domios-owned entry and its owned secret; foreign entries and secrets are preserved.

Connection tests have a ten-second failure deadline and return models or typed `timeout`, `unauthorized`, `connection`, or `invalid_response` errors. Configuration and secret-store refusals are also typed; returned errors omit keys and remote response bodies.

Presets map a name to a model, prompt and optional parameters (temperature 0–2, top-p 0–1, steps 1–10000). They are Domios-owned OpenCode agents; foreign agents cannot be overwritten or removed. Select a preset in New Session or with `agent spawn --preset`; conflicting model or agent launch arguments are refused. Recorded launch parameters preserve the preset on restart/resume. Provider and preset changes emit versioned catalogue events, so the picker and model chip refresh without a reload. OpenCode model variants appear as reasoning levels and travel with launch and live model switching; the chip identifies the live or restart/resume path.

### Secret store

Pluggable secret store for the `domios mem secret` command family and the Settings → Secrets UI. Configure the active backend, (for Bitwarden) the default org/collection that new items land in, and (for Bitwarden) the server URL. Auto-unlock is not a config key: a secret-backend plugin opts in through its manifest and the unlock request (see the secret-store reference below).

```toml
[integrations.secrets]
backend = "local"                # "local" (default), "bitwarden", or "mock"
default_organization = ""        # Default org id for new items (Bitwarden); empty = personal vault
default_collection = ""          # Default collection id for new items (Bitwarden)

[integrations.secrets.bitwarden]
server_url = "https://vault.bitwarden.com"   # Public vault, or self-hosted Vaultwarden URL
```

Backends:
- `local` (default) — a plaintext JSON file at `<data_dir>/.secrets` (`~/.domios/.secrets`; dev `~/.domios-dev/.secrets`), mode `0600` on Unix. Values are **not encrypted** and do **not** use the OS keychain; treat the file like an `.env`. A metadata-only index (names, ids, folders, timestamps) lives at `<data_dir>/secrets/local-index.json`. Offline, no external service.
- `bitwarden` — shells out to the official `bw` CLI. Install with `brew install bitwarden-cli` (macOS), `npm i -g @bitwarden/cli` (Linux/cross-platform), or `scoop install bitwarden-cli` (Windows). When `bw` is missing the Settings → Secrets page shows the install hint, an "Install Bitwarden CLI" button, and the CLI returns exit code 6 (backend unavailable). Supports `vault.bitwarden.com` and self-hosted Vaultwarden via `server_url`.
- `mock` — in-memory only. Anything you save is lost on daemon restart. Use for dev / screenshots / tests.

A secret-backend plugin keeps its persisted session and any remembered credential in its own host bucket (service `codeterm.plugin.<plugin-id>`), which uses the same plaintext local file as the `local` backend. Nothing here uses the OS keychain.

**Secrets do not cross the mesh.** `domios --mesh PEER mem secret …` exits with code 7 and a clear error. The vault is local to the machine that holds it.

Full secret-store reference, including CLI, storage internals, error mapping, and plugin authoring: `domios docs SECRETS`.

Settings UI: Settings > Secrets — backend picker, server URL + Apply (Bitwarden), Install Bitwarden CLI button (when `bw` missing), login (password or API key), default scope, recently saved items, lock / sign-out.

# BROWSER: how agents use the Domios browser

Every verb is `domios plugin browser <verb> [args]`. This guide is what `domios docs BROWSER` and `domios plugin browser help` print.

## When to use it

- Verify a web UI you changed in the real running app, instead of claiming it works.
- Reproduce a bug a user reported on a web page, and collect evidence.
- Do a web task the user asked for, such as reading a page or filling a form, while the user can watch.

This is the browser for any web page task in Domios. Use it instead of Chrome extensions, global browser skills or other browser tools.

Do not use it to fetch plain data an HTTP request or an API returns. Use `curl` or the API for that.

## Your browser

- **Ownership.** `open` gives you your own browser. It is named `<YourName>'s Browser`, the user sees it live as a tab nested under yours, and other agents in your workspace may use it too. It closes when you close it with `close`, when your Tab closes, or when your Team closes.
- **Profiles.**
  - Default: a **temporary session**. Opening an agent browser does not create a named persistent profile.
  - An explicit `open --profile clean` uses a throwaway profile.
  - A **named profile** keeps logins and cookies across restarts. The user creates general profiles through the Browser profile menu. Agents may select existing profiles with `open --profile NAME`; an unknown name fails. For DEV QA, agents create origin-bound profiles with the named session commands below, list them with `profile list` and remove inactive profiles with `profile remove NAME`. Never publish, buy, delete or send messages without the user's explicit instruction.
- **One profile across tabs.** Tabs using the same named profile share cookies and logins, with independent pages and controls. Closing one browser leaves the others open.
- **Another agent's browser.** Add `--of <agent>` (its Tab title or tab id) to any verb to act in that agent's browser instead of yours, for example `snapshot --of Snake` then `click button "Continue" --of Snake`. Its owner sees your name on the activity. It must already be open, you cannot `close` it, and refs come from the latest `snapshot` of that browser.
- **Pointing an owner at something.** `annotate <ref> "comment" --of <agent>` (or `annotate button "Sign in" "comment" --of <agent>`, optional `--intent question|change|bug`) sends that agent the same element card the user's point-and-ask sends, signed with your name. It only targets another agent's browser.
- **Shared view.** The user may press *Take control* and click or type alongside you. You are not blocked and not told. Always re-read the page before acting.

## The loop: snapshot, act, re-snapshot

The user can press **Take control** to drag-select page text, interact with forms and scroll. Ctrl/Cmd+C copies the remote selection and Ctrl/Cmd+V inserts local clipboard text. The toolbar also has Copy selected text and Paste text actions. User input invalidates agent refs, so take a fresh snapshot before continuing after the user interacts.

1. `snapshot`: read the page as an accessibility tree with roles, names, control states and element refs. Copy the exact ref shown, including its capture prefix; never construct one from an element's position. **This is the default way to understand a page.**
2. Act on what the snapshot shows, by ref or by role and name:
   - `click button "Sign in"` or `click <exact-ref-from-snapshot>`
   - `type textbox "Email" "me@example.com"` or `type <exact-ref-from-snapshot> "me@example.com"`
   - `press Enter`, `press a ctrl`
   - `goto <url>`, `back`, `forward`, `reload`, `scroll 800`
3. Run `snapshot` again after every navigation or visible change. Elements you saw before may be gone or changed.

Rules:
- Start with `status`. If no browser is open, run `open` before concluding the browser is unavailable.
- Re-snapshot after navigation, clicks that change the page, and any stale-reference error. Every new snapshot issues new refs; full/SPA navigation and viewer input invalidate the previous capture. Navigation, viewer input or a newer capture during a snapshot make the earlier capture fail rather than publishing its refs.
- Role/name locators prefer an exact name, then a substring. If multiple elements match, the command refuses to choose and lists candidate refs; use the intended element's exact ref.
- Control states include `checked`, `selected`, `expanded`, `disabled`, `required`, `readonly`, `focused` and `invalid` when the page exposes them. Use these as evidence when checking a form or toggle.
- `snapshot [limit]` defaults to 200 lines and is capped at 2000. A truncation notice means more content remains; refs are only issued for included elements.
- Prefer refs and role + name from the snapshot over coordinates or CSS selectors.
- After async page changes, wait on evidence (`wait --text T`, `wait --url U`, `wait --selector S`), never on a bare timeout. A wait fails after 15 seconds.
- For secrets, pipe the exact text to `domios plugin browser type <target> --stdin`. Browser masks the input before insertion and redacts the value from output, snapshots, events and annotations. This requires an HTML input that supports password masking. Never put secrets in arguments or print them.
- `type` focuses the element, clears it, then inserts the text. If a custom input still ignores it, click it first and retry.
- Use `text [limit]` to read long content; use `screenshot [file] [--full]` **only for visual claims** (layout, colour, clipping, alignment). Screenshots go to your pad; show one to the user with `@ct-image <path>`.
- **Never report an action as done unless the page proves it.** Re-snapshot and quote the evidence: a new heading, a success message, the changed value. If an action could have sent, submitted, bought or deleted something and you could not read back the result, say the effect is unproven.
- If a command fails, read its error and retry with corrected arguments when the error is actionable. Don't switch to another browser tool (global browser skills, standalone Playwright, a REPL) just because the first call failed.
- Report flaky behaviour as flaky, not as a pass.

## When the page needs the user

`status` shows `needs human` other than `none`, and you should stop and tell the user, when:
- the page shows a bot check or captcha;
- a login is required that you were not given;
- a cookie or consent dialog you may not decide on;
- a native file picker or permission prompt;
- a JavaScript dialog.

Say exactly what is blocking. The user can solve it with *Take control*; then re-snapshot and continue.

## The user can point at things

The user can pick an element in the live view and send a question, change request or bug about it. It arrives in your chat as a Domios notice. If you missed it, `inbox` lists the ones not delivered or read yet (`inbox all` lists every kept one). Each annotation gives you:
- the page;
- the element's role and name, its selector, and its React component (and source file on dev builds);
- its text, attributes, computed styles and box;
- nearby text;
- a cropped screenshot;
- the user's words and intent.

Treat it as a precise pointer: find the code behind the element, answer or change it, then verify in the browser.

## Testing your own web app

1. Start the app's dev server in a `--purpose dev` utility shell, or reuse a running one.
2. `goto http://localhost:<port>`.
3. Walk the user journey you changed, snapshotting after each step.
4. Prove the end state, not just the click. For example, the item appears in the list after reload.
5. Save screenshots for the visual parts and cite them in your report.
6. For each check that passed by hand, propose an automated test (file, framework, assertion).

## Other verbs

- `profiles`: the current profile and the named ones available.
- `endpoint`: the browser's local CDP endpoint, for tools that need it.
- `close`: close your browser.

## Device viewport and capture metrics

`viewport set 390 844 --mobile --dpr 2` applies mobile device metrics to your owned target. Attached application targets refuse device emulation. Viewer resizing preserves the mobile mode.

`screenshot phone.png --viewport 390x844 --mobile --dpr 2 --restore --metrics-json` captures at the requested size and reports the saved path, layout width, content width and CDP layout metrics as JSON. `--restore` restores the previous device metrics even when capture fails; restoration failure is reported explicitly. Without `--restore`, requested metrics stay active.

## Scoped atomic actions

`click --within 'dialog:Settings' --role button --name Save` and `fill --within 'form:Composer' --role textbox --name Message --text 'hello'` resolve exact role/name matches from a fresh accessibility snapshot at action time. Missing, ambiguous, stale, hidden and disabled targets refuse with a reason code. The page performs the action in one JavaScript turn only if its document and mutation/input epoch still match the capture. An `action_unconfirmed` result means the action may have happened: inspect the page, never replay it.

## Bounded structured snapshots

`snapshot --json --scope dialog --actions-only --max-items 30` returns a JSON object with `page`, `scope`, `items`, `truncated` and `maxItems`. Items contain role, bounded name/text, depth and an optional reference. Only included actions receive references. The maximum is 2000 items; `truncated: true` explicitly marks omitted content.

Scopes select one subtree: `dialog`, `sidebar` (complementary landmark), `composer` (form named Composer), or an exact `role:name`. Ambiguous scopes refuse. Password/token inputs and `data-sensitive` subtrees have their values and names redacted in text and JSON snapshots. A failed DOM redaction capture refuses the snapshot.

## Named DEV instance sessions and cleanup

`open --profile dev-qa --origin http://localhost:7686 --expect-build FULL_SHA` creates or reuses a profile bound to that exact origin, opens its `/web/` UI, and refuses a different origin or an unexpected `/api/health` build SHA. `attach` takes the same options and reuses the owned named session. Origins must be bare HTTP(S) origins without credentials, paths, queries or fragments. Existing unbound user profiles cannot be adopted as per-instance profiles.

`connect --profile dev-qa --origin http://localhost:7686 --expect-build FULL_SHA --stdin` opens the session and accepts the instance API token through piped stdin. Never place the token in argv, a URL or a log. The helper stores and reads back the origin-specific token, then reloads; use snapshot evidence to verify authentication. It never reads an inherited host endpoint or token.

`--ephemeral` on open/attach/connect creates a session profile deleted when its last browser closes. An existing persistent profile cannot become ephemeral. `profile list` lists named profiles; `profile remove dev-qa` refuses while a browser still uses it.

At the end of a QA run, close ephemeral sessions. For a persistent per-instance session, run `open --profile clean`, then `profile remove dev-qa`, then `close`. Remove each per-instance profile used by the run.

Native file picker driving returns `unsupported` on all platforms, including Windows: the current host has no lifecycle-owned native dialog handle or file chooser interception. Use Take control to choose files in a dialog the page opened.

## Accessible state waits

`wait --role button --name 'Aria-only label' --state enabled --timeout 15s` uses Chromium's accessibility tree and its computed accessible names, including aria-only labels. States are `visible`, `hidden`, `enabled` and `expanded`. Hidden also succeeds when no matching accessible element remains; ambiguous matches refuse. Durations use `ms`, `s` or `m`, default to 15s, and are capped at 2m. DOM mutation and input events wake the check; elapsed time only bounds failure. Navigation during a pending wait returns `stale`.

## Disclosure controls

Snapshots issue actionable refs for Chromium `DisclosureTriangle` controls (`summary` is a role alias). `expand summary 'Details'` and `collapse summary 'Details'` capture the current control, click only when its expanded state differs, then re-read the accessibility tree to confirm the requested state. Already matching state succeeds without a click. Ambiguous or stale controls refuse; `action_unconfirmed` or `state_unconfirmed` never triggers a replay.

## QA convenience commands

`open --domios-instance qa --api-port 7790 [--ephemeral]` checks the loopback daemon's exact instance name, API port and DEV application identifier, reads that named DEV instance's protected local credential internally, and connects using an automatically named origin-bound profile. The caller supplies no token. It refuses production port 7685, missing credentials and identity mismatches. Names are lowercase slugs. This convenience path uses the standard named DEV data directory and ignores inherited data-directory/host/token overrides; custom data roots can use the explicit named-session and stdin helper above.

`snapshot --with-text --max-items 80` adds bounded static accessibility leaf text, such as description values and list-item text. It can accompany `--json`, `--scope` and `--actions-only`; static text gets no action refs and sensitive subtrees stay redacted.

`wait --role switch --name Ligatures --state checked` and `--state unchecked` wait for explicit AX checked state. `pressed`, `unpressed`, `selected` and `unselected` use their corresponding AX properties. Missing or mixed values satisfy neither positive nor negative predicates.

`snapshot --json --with-text --out evidence/page.json` and `text 12000 --out evidence/page.txt` save redacted output directly into the calling agent's pad and return its path. Relative paths resolve against the caller's pad, including with `--of`. Absolute paths must remain inside that pad. Parent traversal, symlinks/reparse points and Windows device names refuse.
